sentence: Lupus symptoms vary from person to person.
The NHS lists joint and muscle pain and extreme tiredness that does not go away however much a person rests as main symptoms.
A rash often appears across the nose and cheeks and can be triggered by sunlight.
NIAMS describes this as a butterfly-shaped rash.
Other possible signs include headaches, mouth ulcers, fever, hair loss, weight loss and swollen glands.
Some people have Raynaud's, where the fingers and toes change colour.
Arthritis in lupus can cause painful, swollen joints and morning stiffness.
The NHS says lupus often flares up, with symptoms becoming worse for a few weeks or sometimes longer.
Lupus can also affect organs such as the kidneys, heart, lungs and brain.
Lupus is an autoimmune condition, which means the immune system attacks healthy tissue.
Lupus UK explains that the immune system becomes overactive and makes antibodies against the body's own cells, and inflammation can then affect the skin, joints and other tissues.
The NHS says lupus is not contagious.
The causes are not fully understood, but the NHS lists possible triggers including viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause.
The NHS says lupus is more common in women and in people of African, Caribbean, Asian or Chinese background.
Lupus UK describes the course as variable, with flares and remission, and says the disease lasts many years in most people.
Because the symptoms overlap with other conditions, diagnosis can take time.
No single test confirms lupus, and doctors combine the person's history, a physical examination and laboratory tests.
A GP usually starts with blood tests.
NIAMS says a positive ANA (antinuclear antibody) test is common in lupus but does not confirm it, because healthy people can also have a positive result.
The NHS says lupus may be diagnosed if tests show a high level of a certain type of antibody and the person also has the typical symptoms.
NIDDK says lupus nephritis, which is kidney involvement, is diagnosed through urine and blood tests and sometimes a kidney biopsy.
Scans of the heart, kidneys or other organs may follow if they seem to be affected.
There is no cure for lupus, but the NHS says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early.
Lupus UK says treatment aims to keep the disease controlled to reduce the chance of a flare.
Options named by the NHS include anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, hydroxychloroquine for fatigue, skin and joint problems, and steroids for kidney inflammation and rashes.
For severe cases, immunosuppressant or biological medicines may be used.
NIAMS mentions a biologic medicine that blocks the type I interferon receptor and may improve skin, joint and overall lupus symptoms.
NIAMS advises working with a doctor to decide the best treatment plan and taking medicines as prescribed.
The NHS self-care advice for people with lupus includes sun protection, pacing yourself, staying active and managing stress.
Lupus UK describes the course as variable.
Some people have one flare, while others have periods of increased disease activity followed by remission, and many flares are mild.
NIAMS lists increased tiredness, joint swelling, pain, rash, fever, abdominal pain and headache as common warning signs of a flare.
It says spotting these warning signs can help a person prevent a flare or make the symptoms less severe, and that sun exposure and stress can trigger flares.
The NHS self-care advice includes sun protection, pacing yourself, staying active and managing stress.
Sun protection includes a high-factor sunscreen and a hat.
NHS 111 Wales also advises against smoking, which it says makes lupus worse.
NIAMS says many people with lupus lead happy lives.
Severity varies, and a severe case can cause serious inflammation of the heart, lungs, brain or kidneys.
Lupus nephritis is inflammation of the kidneys, and Great Ormond Street Hospital says it can in a few cases progress to kidney failure.
Lupus UK says kidney disease in lupus needs careful monitoring because it can cause no symptoms, and NIDDK says it is found through urine and blood tests and sometimes a biopsy.
Lupus UK says many women with lupus have successful pregnancies, and that stable disease before conception makes a stable pregnancy more likely.

It also says lupus pregnancies can sometimes end in miscarriage or stillbirth, that some women have flares during pregnancy and need careful observation, and that lupus may sometimes affect fertility.
Lupus UK also discusses pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy complication, and advises that individual pregnancy questions are discussed with a specialist.
No, lupus is not contagious.
It is an autoimmune condition, in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue.
The exact trigger is unclear, but the NHS lists possible contributors including viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause.
These are possible contributors to developing lupus, not ways of catching it from another person.
There is no cure for lupus, according to the NHS.
The NHS says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early.
Lupus UK says treatment aims to keep the disease controlled to reduce the chance of a flare.
The NHS lists anti-inflammatory painkillers, hydroxychloroquine and steroids, with immunosuppressant or biological medicines for severe cases.
Lupus UK says the outlook for survival has improved in recent years, and that with early treatment lupus may settle and ultimately go into remission.
The course is variable: some people have one flare, while others have periodic increased disease activity followed by remission.
A rheumatologist or lupus specialist can discuss what this means for an individual.
Lupus UK says many women with lupus have successful pregnancies, and that stable disease before conception makes a stable pregnancy more likely.
It also says lupus pregnancies can sometimes end in miscarriage or stillbirth, and that some women have flares during pregnancy and need careful observation.
Questions about pregnancy are best discussed with a rheumatologist or lupus specialist.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if lupus symptoms occur often, and says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early.
Joint and muscle pain, extreme tiredness that rest does not ease, and a rash across the nose and cheeks are among the main symptoms.
A routine GP appointment is the usual first step.
Severe or sudden symptoms, such as chest pain, need urgent help through NHS 111 or the GP the same day, or 999 in an emergency.
